title: A&E did not get the basics right - now my son's life is ruined at 32

input.lead: Oli's experience is one of a growing number of clinical negligence claims being made in England, BBC analysis shows
input.summary: Oli's experience is one of a growing number of clinical negligence claims being made in England, BBC analysis shows
input.evidence_text: Health correspondent Published 3 hours ago In May 2024, a few months after having treatment for a brain tumour, Oli Coppock went to Warrington Hospital's emergency department with bad headaches and dizziness He underwent tests and assessments, but did not have a brain scan, before going home. It was a decision that ultimately ruined his life at the age of 32, his family says. A week later, with fluid building up on the brain, he suffered a cardiac arrest. He did not recover and now l Oli's case is just one of a growing number of clinical negligence claims being made in England relating to A&E care. An analysis by the BBC shows there has been a 41% rise in cases over the past five years, with doctors linking it to the long delays and pressures being seen in em Oli's father, Stephen, says he knows A&E staff are under pressure, but he cannot understand how a brain scan was not ordered, given his son's medical history Despite the brain tumour and a recent diagnosis of multiple sclerosis, Oli was otherwise fit and well and positive about his future. He had a career in digital marketing, loved going to the gym and did some DJing in his spare time Stephen says the whole family – including Oli's six siblings - has been left "angry and broken" by what happened to him

title: Garry Bridges sets out priorities as Manchester council leader

input.summary: Garry Bridges also discussed rough sleeping, high-rise development and the city's G20 hopes
input.evidence_text: Manchester's new council leader has said delivering more homes is an "absolute priority" as he set out his ambitions for the city Garry Bridges told BBC Radio Manchester's Joe McGrath Breakfast Show that high-rise developments had a place in Manchester's housing mix, but were not affordable to everyone The council aims to help deliver 36,000 homes by 2032, including at least 10,000 social, council or genuinely affordable homes. The council said almost a quarter of the affordable homes target had already been met Bridges also described rough sleeping as a "complete failure of the state and of society", with the council expecting about £2m through the government's £442m Rough Sleeping Programme Bridges, who was formally appointed council leader last week after succeeding Bev Craig, said getting the job had taken "a good few days to sink in" He described it as an "amazing honour" and said becoming leader was not something he had imagined when he first became involved in politics

title: Greater Manchester hospital staff strike again over overtime

input.lead: More than 350 staff at four Greater Manchester hospitals are due to walk out later this month
input.summary: More than 350 staff at four Greater Manchester hospitals are due to walk out later this month
input.evidence_text: Greater Manchester hospital staff strike again over overtime - BBC News Image source, Dixon/Geograph Image caption, Salford Royal Hospital is one of four Manchester sites affected By Haider Saleem North West , Reporting from Norht West Published 7 September 2026 More than 350 staff at four Greater Manchester hospitals are set to strike again in an ongoing row about overtime payments. Unison said talks had stalled and claimed the Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust had rejected offers to resume negotiations. The workers, including operating theatre staff at Salford Royal Hospital, Royal Oldham Hospital, Rochdale Infirmary and Fairfield Hospital in Bury, will strike on 14, 15 and 17 September. The latest action follows previous strikes in June and August. The trust said it would do "everything it can to minimise the impact on patients and maintain high standards of care and quality at all times". 'Chronically under-staffed' The dispute centres on the use of NHS Professionals to manage overtime. Unison said staff could earn less for some overtime shifts than they would on a normal shift, with some workers missing out on as much as £80. The union's North West regional organiser Kevin Dolan said the trust had given "no indication that it's willing to re-enter negotiations". Dolan also said operating theatre services were "chronically under-staffed" and staff were choosing to work extra shifts to cover shortages. Unison said the new walkouts would take the total number of strike days since June to 10 if no agreement was reached. Ahead of the August strikes, the trust declared a critical incident to help it secure extra support and keep urgent surgery running. It said some procedures would be postponed. input.evidence_text: How Hollyoaks saved the life of Manchester mental health activist - BBC News Image source, John Junior Image caption, "I felt like I couldn't tell anyone how I felt," John said. "I want others to hear my story and to know help is out there." By Georgie Docker North West Published 7 September 2026 A mental health campaigner said they were seconds away from taking their own life before being saved by a plotline in a soap opera. John Junior, 37, from Wythenshawe, in Greater Manchester, had been suffering with depression since the age of 14. But after the sudden death of their father in 2018, the then-IT worker said they hit rock bottom. During lockdown in 2020, John was contemplating taking their own life when a Hollyoaks storyline stopped them in their tracks. "I seconds away from ending my life," John recalled. "I had Hollyoaks on in the background and I turned round to watch the scene. "There was a moment when a character was told her partner had taken his own life. "Something happened to me and it gave me enough time to think beyond what I was about to do. "I wouldn't be here today if it wasn't for Hollyoaks." Ahead of World Suicide Prevention Day 2026, on 10 September, John said now they want to share their experience to encourage others to speak out. title: Bolton schoolfriends set to reunite after 60 years

input.lead: Two friends have spent the past two years tracking down former classmates from a Bolton high school
input.summary: Two friends have spent the past two years tracking down former classmates from a Bolton high school
input.evidence_text: For children starting a new secondary school this year social media means they will likely always have a way of keeping in touch with friends after they leave But for past generations it was very different. Often the last day of school was the last time you saw most class mates - even if you might not realise it at the time It was something that prompted grandmother Karen Feay to track down the people she started Rivington & Blackrod Grammar School in Bolton with 60 years ago "I bumped into an old school friend and we got talking about our school memories - and it snowballed from there," she said. "We all started in 1966 which makes everyone 70 or 71 years old now." Karen and her friend Susan Hart have spent the past two years tracking down fellow school mates on social media A task she said had been more difficult for women who had changed their surnames after getting married

title: The skull of a saint that was discovered during renovations

input.lead: Ambrose Barlow was found guilty of treason and sentenced to death in 1641
input.summary: Ambrose Barlow was found guilty of treason and sentenced to death in 1641
input.evidence_text: On 25 April 1641, Ambrose Barlow celebrated a secret Easter Sunday mass at Morleys Hall near Astley in Greater Manchester But, by the end of the service, the building had been surrounded by a 400-strong armed group led by a local vicar "King Charles I issued a decree stating that all Catholic priests must leave within a month...and if they didn't, they would face the consequences of treason," said the Right Reverend John Arnold, the Bishop of Salford King Charles I wanted to prove that he supported the Protestant faith while keeping his political enemies at bay as parliament were suspicious of his Catholic wife The congregation urged Ambrose Barlow to hide but Arnold said he refused and instead ordered the doors to be opened and surrendered peacefully "He didn't make any attempt to avoid arrest," said Arnold
